prompt: What does fine-tuning change that a prompt does not?
hint: Look at the two rows of the figure.

choices.text: The model's weights
choices.why: Right. A prompt is new text on every request; fine-tuning produces a model whose weights are different.

choices.text: The text sent with each request, which is rewritten automatically for you
choices.why: That is what a prompt changes. Fine-tuning changes the model the text is sent to.

choices.text: The sampling settings, such as the temperature
choices.why: Those are set per request, lessons 13 to 17. Neither technique is about them.

choices.text: The tokenizer the model uses to read text
choices.why: The tokenizer stays as it is. Fine-tuning adjusts the weights.

prompt: The café changes its opening hours every season. A colleague wants to fine-tune a model on the handbook so it knows them. What is the problem?
hint: What happens to a fact once it is spread across the weights?

choices.text: Nothing, since fine-tuning is how a model learns facts
choices.why: It is the thing fine-tuning does worst: facts trained in cannot be updated or removed on their own.

choices.text: Fine-tuning works on style only, so the model ignores the hours entirely
choices.why: It does learn from them, which is part of the problem: it learns them and then they go stale.

choices.text: Handbooks are too short to fine-tune on
choices.why: Length is not the issue. The issue is that the facts change.

choices.text: Every change means training again
choices.why: Right, and the old hours stay mixed into the weights. Facts that change belong in the prompt, fetched when needed, which is lesson 11.

prompt: Which of these is a good reason to fine-tune?
hint: What is fine-tuning good at: habits, or facts?

choices.text: The model does not know this week's prices
choices.why: Prices that change belong in the prompt. Training them in makes them stale.

choices.text: Nobody on the team agrees on what a good answer looks like
choices.why: Then nobody can write the examples. Decide first.

choices.text: One house style across millions of support replies
choices.why: Right. A consistent style at large volume is a habit, and habits are what training on examples builds.

choices.text: The model answered one question wrongly once
choices.why: One wrong answer is a reason to look at the prompt, not to train a new model.

prompt: A team fine-tunes on 2,000 labelled messages, and the model still sorts messages inconsistently. The labels were written by five people who never agreed on the categories. What went wrong?
hint: What did the model learn from?

choices.text: 2,000 examples is too few for any fine-tuning job
choices.why: The number is not the problem here. Consistent labels are.

choices.text: It learnt the inconsistency that was in the examples
choices.why: Right. Training makes likely what the examples show. Inconsistent examples teach inconsistency; the categories had to be decided first.

choices.text: The base model was too small to learn categories
choices.why: Size did not cause this. The examples contradicted each other.

choices.text: Fine-tuning cannot learn a classification task
choices.why: Sorting into categories is one of the things it does well, given consistent examples.

prompt: Fine-tuning is training ___ on your own examples: the weights are nudged towards making your answers more likely.
Which of these is fine-tuning good at? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Answering in one fixed JSON format every time
choices.why: Yes. A format is a habit, and training on examples builds habits.

choices.text: Making a long prompt unnecessary for a narrow task
choices.why: Yes. Instructions a prompt carried on every request are carried by the weights instead.

choices.text: Keeping up with prices that change every week
choices.why: Facts that change belong in the prompt. Trained in, they go stale.

choices.text: Deciding what a good answer should be
choices.why: Nobody can write the examples until that is decided.

choices.text: One question, which the model answers during training
choices.why: The model does not answer anything you keep. The answer is part of the example.

choices.text: A rule the model reads before every request it receives
choices.why: Training data is not sent with requests. It shapes the weights once.

choices.text: A score for how good a reply was
choices.why: There is no score in the line. There is a message and the right reply.

choices.text: One conversation, with the answer you decided is right
choices.why: Right. Each line is a user message and the assistant reply the model should learn to give.

prompt: `tok count` gave `few-shot.txt` and `short.txt`. How many more tokens does the few-shot prompt send on every request?
hint: Subtract one count from the other.

prompt: At the illustrative prices, 10,000 requests cost 4.33 with the few-shot prompt and 0.53 with the short one. How much is saved per 10,000 requests?
The `tok cost` capture shows a saving per request. What does this lesson say about it?
hint: Compare it to the other costs.

choices.text: It proves fine-tuning is always cheaper
choices.why: It shows one line of the bill. Data collection, training runs, evaluation and hosting are not in it.

choices.text: It is real and small, and fine-tuning's costs are large and paid first
choices.why: Right. The saving matters at very large volume, and only after the costs of data, training and evaluation are paid.

choices.text: It is fake, since the prices are made up
choices.why: The prices are illustrative; the token counts are real. The comparison holds at any price.

choices.text: It shows fine-tuned models cost nothing per token
choices.why: The short prompt still costs per token. It costs less because it is shorter.

prompt: Which cost of fine-tuning is usually the largest?
hint: Who has to check every example?

choices.text: Collecting and labelling the examples
choices.why: Right. Hundreds or thousands of examples, each one checked by a person who knows the answer.

choices.text: The tokens of the training file
choices.why: Training is billed, but the people writing and checking the data cost more.

choices.text: Sending the shorter prompt
choices.why: That is the cheap part, and the reason to fine-tune at all.

choices.text: Downloading the base model to the provider
choices.why: There is no such download in a hosted fine-tuning job.

prompt: Your provider retires the base model your fine-tuned model was built on. What does this lesson say happens?
hint: What is a fine-tuned model tied to?

choices.text: Nothing: the fine-tuned weights carry over to the new model on their own
choices.why: Weights belong to one architecture and one starting point. They do not carry over.

choices.text: You keep using it, since retired models run for ever
choices.why: A retired model stops being served. That is what retiring means.

choices.text: You only need to rewrite the prompt
choices.why: The prompt was the cheap part. The training was tied to the old base.

choices.text: Start again on a new base model
choices.why: Right: data, training and evaluation are repeated. A prompt moves to a new model by being sent to it; a fine-tuned model does not move at all.

prompt: Why does fine-tuning need an evaluation set the model never trained on?
hint: How would you know a run helped?

choices.text: Because the provider refuses to train without one
choices.why: Some services ask for one; the reason to have it is yours, not theirs.

choices.text: To make the training file longer
choices.why: Its whole point is that it stays out of training.

choices.text: To teach the model the answers a second time
choices.why: If the model trained on it, it could not show anything.

choices.text: To show the run helped
choices.why: Right. Without held-back examples you cannot tell a good run from a bad one.

prompt: Put the ladder in the order this lesson says to try things.
Match each problem to what to try first.

pairs.left: it does not know your current prices
a prompt that works costs too much at huge volume
nobody agrees what a good answer is

prompt: A start-up's chatbot answers questions about its product, which ships a new version every two weeks. Answers about new features are wrong. Which rung of the ladder fits?
hint: Is the problem a habit or knowledge?

choices.text: Retrieval of the current docs per question
choices.why: Right. The problem is knowledge that changes, and only retrieval keeps up without retraining.

choices.text: Fine-tuning on the documentation every two weeks
choices.why: Possible, and the most expensive way to stay two weeks behind. Facts that change are retrieval's job.

choices.text: Adding three worked examples to the prompt
choices.why: Examples teach a format or a style. They do not supply this fortnight's features.

choices.text: A clearer instruction telling it to be accurate
choices.why: Wording cannot supply facts the model never saw.

prompt: A prompt with eleven examples sorts tickets well. The team handles a few hundred tickets a month. Should they fine-tune?
hint: Run the arithmetic of the cost section at this volume.

choices.text: No: the saving at that volume will not pay for data, training and evaluation
choices.why: Right. The prompt works; fine-tuning pays off at very large volume, and this is not that.

choices.text: Yes, since fine-tuning gives better answers than examples
choices.why: Not necessarily, and the examples already work. The question is cost, and the volume is small.

choices.text: Yes, because a long prompt is a sign of a bad prompt
choices.why: Length is a cost, not a defect. At this volume the cost is tiny.

choices.text: No, since fine-tuning cannot sort tickets
choices.why: Sorting tickets is a good fine-tuning task. It is just not worth it here.

prompt: What does a prompt have that a fine-tuned model does not?
hint: Think about the last two bullets of the costs.

choices.text: It changes the weights, and more precisely than training does
choices.why: A prompt does not change the weights at all.

choices.text: It costs nothing per request
choices.why: Every token of a prompt is billed, as `tok cost` showed.

choices.text: It cannot be read by the model's provider
choices.why: A prompt is sent to the provider with every request.

choices.text: It moves to a new model by being sent to it
choices.why: Right. It changes in a minute and needs no training, hosting or re-training.
